extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent practitioners advising clients on Canadian filings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical summary of the one-year inventor disclosure 'grace period' under the Canadian Patent Act, differences from (pre- and post-AIA) U.S. law, and consequences for filing strategy in Canada and the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory one-year grace for novelty (paragraph 28.2(1)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 28.2(1)(a) of the Canadian Patent Act: the claimed invention in the Canadian patent application must not have been disclosed more than one year before the filing date by the applicant, or by a person who obtained knowledge, directly or indirectly, from the applicant, in such a manner that the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: (a) the provision creates a one-year grace period for disclosures made by the applicant (or those who obtained knowledge from the applicant); (b) the one-year period runs from the Canadian filing date (not the priority date); (c) for PCT national phase entries, the Canadian filing date is deemed to be the PCT international filing date. Practitioners should note the precise statutory wording when assessing whether a disclosure falls within the grace window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory one-year grace for obviousness (section 28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 28.3 of the Canadian Patent Act, governing obviousness, contains a similar one-year provision to paragraph 28.2(1)(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act treats novelty and obviousness similarly with respect to applicant-originated disclosures; analyze both novelty and obviousness issues under the one-year framework when evaluating prior disclosures by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any disclosure in which 'the subject-matter became available to the public in Canada or elsewhere' will trigger the start of the one-year grace period in Canada. Thus, the disclosure must be a public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-public/confidential disclosures (for example under a non-disclosure agreement) do not trigger the one-year period. The public disclosure can be in any form (written, oral, use, etc.) and can occur anywhere in the world; there are no geographic restrictions under Canadian law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior public use or public sale of the invention may or may not be a public disclosure that will trigger the start of the one-year grace period; to qualify, the public use or sale must be an 'enabling' disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is 'enabling' usually turns on the facts: 'if a person skilled in the art would be enabled to arrive at the invention from the disclosure without exercising inventive skill or undue burden, then the disclosure is enabling.' Example: a sold product that can be discovered by routine reverse engineering is likely an enabling disclosure. Case law: Canwell Enviro-Industries Ltd. v. Baker Petrolite Corp. (2002 FCA 158) discussed this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer for sale follows enabling-disclosure test
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer for sale will only trigger the start of the one-year grace period in Canada if the offer for sale constitutes an enabling public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same enabling-disclosure analysis as for public use/sale. Practitioners should be cautious: whether a particular offer is enabling is fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical safe approach on uses/sales/offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is room for argument, the safest approach is to assume that any prior non-confidential use, sale, or offer for sale of the invention is potentially an enabling public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, file a patent application in Canada within one year of the earliest such use, sale, or offer for sale to preserve rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/scope of 'applicant' for grace-period protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Canadian law, the applicant includes the inventors and the legal representative of the inventors (typically the assignee). The one-year grace period applies to public disclosures made by the applicant, or by another who obtained knowledge, directly or indirectly, from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, disclosures originating from either the inventors or the assignee within the one-year period prior to filing are not citable against the application when assessing novelty or obviousness — even if the assignee's disclosure did not originate from the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation/applicant-derived applications issue and lack of derivation proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Canada does not have derivation proceedings and there is little jurisprudence on whether inventor-derived applications filed by others in the one-year window are citable against an applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Ultraviolet Systems Inc. v. Brasscorp Ltd. (2009 FC 58) — court held a third party's application describing the applicant's earlier disclosure was not citable against the applicant. Nevertheless, because of the absence of formal derivation procedures and sparse jurisprudence, the safe approach is to protect confidential information and minimize reliance on the grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian grace period runs from Canadian filing date (not priority date)
rubrics_metrics.description: The one-year grace period in Canada runs from the filing date in Canada, not the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: filing a U.S. priority application within one year of a disclosure does NOT extend the Canadian grace period. Example scenario in text: a disclosure on June 1, 2010; U.S. filing May 1, 2011 (within one year); filing in Canada on May 1, 2012 would be too late. Practitioners should docket to file in Canada within one year of the first non-confidential disclosure when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: No absolute on-sale bar in Canada
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no absolute on-sale bar in Canada; a sale or offer for sale will only trigger the start of the one-year grace period if it constitutes an enabling public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with (pre-AIA) U.S. law where a sale/offer in the U.S., even if confidential, may trigger the U.S. one-year bar. A confidential sale/offer under NDA might trigger the U.S. on-sale bar but will not trigger Canada's grace period because it is not a public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: No geographic restrictions on Canadian grace-period-triggering disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Canadian law, it does not matter in which country the public disclosure was made, or the form of the public disclosure (written, oral, use, etc.). Any enabling public disclosure will trigger the start of the one-year grace period in Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with pre-AIA U.S. §102(b) where public uses/sales outside the U.S. might not trigger the U.S. one-year period.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA (U.S.) changes and cross-border filing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA introduces changes to U.S. §102 including a one-year grace period with no geographic restrictions and no limitation to forms of disclosure; however, under the AIA the U.S. grace period is calculated back from the priority date, not the U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing strategies arising from the difference: (a) file in Canada within one year of the public disclosure (required by Canadian law) and then file the corresponding U.S. application a year later claiming priority back to the Canadian application — this can delay the start of U.S. patent term; (b) consider accelerated examination in Canada and use favorable Canadian allowance to leverage the Patent Prosecution Highway in the U.S. Practitioners should account for the different reference dates (Canadian filing date vs U.S. priority date) when docketing cross-border filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filing/docketing recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve Canadian rights, U.S. practitioners should consider docketing to file in Canada within one year of the first non-confidential disclosure of the invention, as soon as it is known or suspected that there has been or will be such a disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on docketing to file in Canada within one year of the earliest priority date will not preserve Canadian rights if there has been an enabling public disclosure before the priority application is filed. Take proactive steps (docketing, confidentiality protection, timely national filings) to avoid losing rights in Canada.
